title: Speed-first waves 11-15: real processors and FPGAs (11-13 October)
made_with: AI agents (Claude) directed by the author
machines: one Apple M4 Mac mini (all processor timings); GitHub-hosted Arm Neoverse N2 runners (SEAL port check); open FPGA tools (Yosys, nextpnr), no vendor tools, no board
status_note: For measurements, "checked by computer" means an independent AI critic re-measured the claim with its own baseline and programs (the detail says how many); "one program, not repeated by anyone" means no critic re-ran it. No person repeated any measurement.

bar.processors: at least 10 % less time than the strongest available baseline, like for like, at real sizes
bar.fpgas: at least 10 % less area at equal throughput and clock
bar.or: a capability the baselines lack, with a measured advantage

lessons: Kernel gains are rarely application gains: measure the transform's share of the whole job first (only the SEAL NTT moved a whole application by more than 10 %).
Every headline shrank under a stronger baseline: a better library (FFTW double with NEON and a working timer, KFR), more cores (one matrix unit per cluster), colder caches, or a different design.
Credit the known part: most FPGA wins were a known mechanism in a new use (WP486 packing, vertical CSE, LUT-RAM transposition, carry-cell absorption).
The obvious rewrite takes a large share of the gain: build the fair rival before claiming.

findings.statement: A NEON fp64-FMA NTT in place of SEAL 4.1.2's scalar NTT (primes below 2^50; the loop's two 60-bit primes ran a tuned scalar radix-4 NTT, also new) makes a loop of real CKKS operations at N = 2^14 21.2 % faster, with word-for-word equal ciphertexts, on one core and on all four P-cores. With SEAL's own code for the 60-bit primes the gain was -19.1 % (the developer's run, not repeated by the critic).
findings.status_detail: one critic re-measured it with its own scalar control; a fairness critic read it
findings.conditions: Apple M4, SEAL 4.1.2, CKKS N = 2^14, moduli 60, 7 x 40, 60 bits

findings.statement: SEAL's own BFV default moduli at N = 2^12 to 2^14 are all below 2^50, so the same kernel makes the BFV loop 16.3 % to 20.8 % faster; CKKS at N = 2^15 gains 27.0 % and the tutorial size N = 2^13 (60, 40, 40, 60) only 10.8 %.
findings.status_detail: found by the critic, correcting the developer's "default moduli only -8 %"
supersedes: the developer's claim "SEAL default moduli only -8 %"

findings.statement: A radix-4 scalar NTT with one overflow guard per pass for 55-60-bit primes gives -16.7 % on BFV at N = 2^15 against SEAL as shipped but only -6.3 % against our own scalar control: below the bar.
findings.status_detail: one program, not repeated by anyone (read by the fairness critic only)

findings.statement: An exact 55-60-bit NTT through 16-bit limb products on the M4's matrix unit is 29 % to 49 % slower than a tuned scalar NTT (the whole NTT +37 %): moving partial sums out of the unit and the 87-bit reduction cost more than the products save.
findings.status_detail: one program, not repeated by anyone

findings.statement: The NTT ported into SEAL 4.6.2 as the build setting SEAL_USE_NEON_NTT (off by default, primes below 2^50) passes SEAL's whole test suite with the setting off (372/372) and on (373/373) on the M4 (Release and Debug) and with GCC 13.3 and Clang 18.1 on Arm Neoverse N2; it switches itself off on x86 (372/372 pass); with it off the library objects are byte-identical to unmodified SEAL 4.6.2; the new tests catch 11 of 12 planted bugs.
findings.status_detail: SEAL's own tests on two chips and two compilers; planted bugs; two independent AI skeptics, neither refuted it

findings.statement: The ported NTT is exact: about 36.6 million transforms against SEAL's scalar code gave 0 mismatches; CKKS, BFV and BGV results are byte-identical with the setting on and off in all four rounding modes; the reduction planner was checked with exact rationals in 7,130 cases. The exactness proof itself is a written argument in a code comment.
findings.status_detail: two independent AI skeptics with their own programs, neither refuted it; the written proof is argued by hand, not checked (not in Lean)

findings.statement: With the setting on, SEAL's own benchmark program on the M4 (generic ARMv8.0-A build, SEAL's 128-bit default primes, n = 4,096 to 16,384) runs the NTT 35 % to 58 % faster, relinearisation and rotation 24 % to 30 %, CKKS rescale 30 % to 33 %, BFV decryption 20 % to 26 %, BFV multiplication and squaring 5 % to 9 %, multiply-then-relinearise 7 % to 12 % (BFV) and 21 % to 26 % (CKKS; the sum of the two measured operations); nothing changes at n = 32,768 except BFV batch encoding and decoding (20-bit plaintext prime).
findings.status_detail: one program, not repeated by anyone; 7 off/on pairs; a control with the NEON code switched off at run time matched the rows with an NTT (median gap 0.8 points, at most 4.6)

findings.statement: The apparent 20 % gain on CKKS decryption (which runs no NTT) is not the port; most likely it is where the machine code of the benchmark program happens to sit (an inference from the control runs; the loop was not traced); it also inflates BFV decryption by 3 to 4 points.
findings.status_detail: one program, not repeated by anyone (a control with identical code layout and memory)

findings.statement: On GitHub's Arm machines (Arm Neoverse N2) the gains are smaller: fully reduced forward NTT -27 % to -30 %, public-key encryption -8 % to -15 %, relinearisation and rotation about -4 % to -5 % (GCC) and about -9 % to -10 % (Clang), BFV multiplication -1 % to -3 %; two runs on fresh machines agree within about half a point.
findings.status_detail: one program, not repeated by anyone; two runs, two compilers, 7 pairs each

findings.statement: With GCC at n = 32,768, SEAL's own fully reduced forward NTT runs 3 % to 4 % slower in the build with the setting on although its machine code is identical: the loop's alignment moved.
findings.status_detail: one program, not repeated by anyone (disassembly compared)

findings.statement: A batched complex128 FFT on the M4's matrix unit (radix-8 passes as complex 8 x 8 DFT matrices in fp64 outer products) takes 41 % less time than KFR at 512 points and 44 % less than FFTW double with NEON at 4,096 points, one P-core, batch 64, in cache; -50 % / -52 % from DRAM; only -15 % / -16 % at 1,024 (in cache) / 2,048 (from DRAM); -26 % / -18 % on the whole P-cluster.
findings.status_detail: one critic rebuilt the baselines (KFR); a later rebuild of the strongest FFTW corrected the 4,096 figure
supersedes: -52 % at 4,096 points (against an FFTW plan 17-20 % slow)
findings.rerun_for_this_revision: correctness checks at 512 and 4,096 points identical; broken copy fails

findings.statement: One complex128 angular-spectrum propagation step on one P-core with the matrix unit takes 38 % / 47 % / 62 % less time than FFTW double with NEON and its own 2-D plan, at 1,024^2 / 2,048^2 / 4,096^2 (about -30 / -42 / -56 % with natural-order output, worked out from parts).
findings.status_detail: one critic and the fairness critic
supersedes: -56 / -49 / -62 % against PFFFT-d or KFR-d rows plus transpose

findings.statement: The claimed -19 % for the optics step on the whole P-cluster at 1,024^2 does not hold: it ties FFTW's own 4-thread 2-D plan (in place, PATIENT).
findings.status_detail: refuted by the critic's FFTW 4-thread 2-D plan
findings.refuted_by: FFTW double with NEON, its own 4-thread 2-D plan

findings.statement: On the whole P-cluster the optics step gains 12.7 % / 20.7 % at 2,048^2 / 4,096^2 against four NEON threads running the same strip plan (27-38 % against FFTW's threaded 2-D plan).
findings.status_detail: one critic and the fairness critic

findings.statement: A one-pass fp64 Welch spectrum (window, FFT, |X|^2 accumulation) on one P-core with the matrix unit takes 33 % / 27 % / 11 % / 41 % less time than FFTW double with NEON and the real-input routes, at segment lengths 512 / 1,024 / 2,048 / 4,096, 2^22 samples, 50 % Hann.
findings.status_detail: one critic and the fairness critic

findings.statement: On four P-cores (64 channels) the matrix-unit Welch clears the bar at no segment length (-1 % to -10 %); the claimed -10.3 % and -11.2 % are refuted.
findings.status_detail: refuted by the critic, who added FFTW double with NEON to a race that had only 4 x vDSP at 1,024
findings.refuted_by: critic re-measurement with the strongest 4-thread baselines

findings.statement: From Python the matrix-unit Welch is 62 % / 66 % faster than a 6-line batched rfft Welch with 4 workers in fp64; most of that is doing Welch in C at all.
findings.status_detail: the fairness critic built the 6-line rival

findings.statement: A drop-in for np.convolve / np.correlate computing the direct sum with fp64 Toeplitz tiles on the matrix unit is 74 % / 85 % / 87 % / 81 % / 68 % / 70 % faster than the best of numpy, scipy and vDSP at 9 / 33 / 129 / 257 / 513 / 1,025 taps (whole Python call, 10^6 samples); against a C PFFFT-double overlap-save it wins only below about 450 taps.
findings.status_detail: one program, not repeated by anyone (wave 15 ended before a critic)
findings.rerun_for_this_revision: check.py quick 534/534 PASS; broken copy 4/4 FAIL; NaN pattern identical

findings.statement: In multi-process code a per-cluster try-lock in front of the matrix unit with a NEON fallback gives -17.6 % / -18.9 % on a 4-worker Whisper log-mel (-15 % with 8 workers) and -11 % / -12 % on a 4-worker fp64 FFT against all-NEON; letting every worker enter the unit is 19 % to 41 % slower than all-NEON (slowest 1 % of calls 1.6-2.8 x); a resident owner process fails (9-25 us hand-off).
findings.status_detail: one program, not repeated by anyone (read by the fairness critic only)

findings.statement: A Toeplitz-tile FIR filter on the matrix unit (fp32, one thread, 2^20 samples, in cache, >= ~1,000 outputs per call) takes 59 % / 53 % / 50 % less time than Accelerate sgemm on block-Toeplitz panels at 16 / 64 / 256 taps; it loses on short calls and above about 500-1,000 taps (the critic's estimate from measured parts).
findings.status_detail: two critics independently built the stronger sgemm baseline

findings.statement: A batched 256-point fp32 FFT on the matrix unit is 28 % faster per core than vDSP's DFT at batch 64 (-31 % to -33 % from DRAM) but only 5 % to 12 % faster on the whole chip in cache and no faster from DRAM, and slower at batch 1.
findings.status_detail: one critic

findings.statement: A NEON textbook Walsh-Hadamard transform (fp32, one thread) takes 8 % to 24 % less time than FFHT's NEON code at each of the six sizes tested from 2^8 to 2^22.
findings.status_detail: one program, not repeated by anyone

findings.statement: conda-forge's FFTW 3.3.10 for osx-arm64 and linux-aarch64 contains 0 NEON codelets; Homebrew enables SIMD on Intel only; Debian arm64 has NEON in single precision only. With the same API and plans, conda-forge's osx-arm64 library takes 1.63-1.68 x as long for complex fp64, 1.27-1.38 x for real fp64 and 2.0-2.6 x for fp32 as FFTW built with NEON.
findings.status_detail: one program, not repeated by anyone (a probe no critic read)

findings.statement: pocketfft's batched vector path (the FFT inside numpy and scipy) is 30 % slower than its scalar path at 64 rows of 4,096 complex128 points (3.86 against 2.96 ns per point), in one run.
findings.status_detail: one program, not repeated by anyone, one run

findings.statement: Two 8-bit telescope signals per DSP48E2 multiply in the SKA-Low channeliser: 224 -> 112 DSPs per slice; the halving is Xilinx WP486's known packing; the new part (exact guards from branch coefficient sums, offset through the C port) saves about 17k LUTs per chip and 1.6-2.1 dB of stop-band over the obvious WP486 design.
findings.status_detail: one critic; synthesis only

findings.statement: With tap groups graded by coefficient size, the packed channeliser needs 7 instead of 14 DSPs per signal lane and meets every filter requirement (ripple +-0.19 dB, alias edge -62.1 dB, far stop-band -83.2 dB); worked out for the KU040 chip: -33.4 % of the channeliser's DSPs, -25.6 % of the chip's; on DSP48E1 one variant meets everything at -43 % DSPs.
findings.status_detail: one program, not repeated by anyone (read by the fairness critic); synthesis only; the chip figures are worked out, not placed

findings.statement: Unpacking the two products from one DSP is bit-exact for all 2^28 inputs; a broken copy fails on 41,180,672 of them.
findings.status_detail: exhaustive simulation (Verilator); re-run for this revision

findings.statement: A streaming radix-2^2 SDF FFT with its stage multiplexers folded into Lattice CCU2 carry cells needs about 20 % fewer slices than the best generic RTL on CrossLink-NX at 256 points (-21 % LUT positions measured; ECP5 about 4 points less; NX clock +10 %); only against Yosys, and a Lattice patent may mean Lattice's tools already do it.
findings.status_detail: one critic; open tools only
supersedes: -23.9 % NX against a weaker baseline; -52 % against a published core (dropped)

findings.statement: Packing two real radar channels into one complex FFT in a range-Doppler chain: built and simulated bit-exact (114,688 outputs, 0 mismatches; a broken split fails), but the area table was never written.
findings.status_detail: correctness checked by computer, one program; area not reported (wave 15 cut short)

findings.statement: A folded 4,096-point FFT on the iCE40-UP5K with all arithmetic in 6 SB_MAC16 blocks takes 235 logic cells, 40 % fewer than the best DSP-multiplier rival (393) and 56 % fewer than the obvious design (529), at 50 MHz (the datasheet cap); 1.85 M samples/s at 48 MHz.
findings.status_detail: one critic (10 seeds, re-timed DSP paths)

findings.statement: A 25-bit folded 8,192-point FFT on the UP5K takes 274 cells, reads a -90 dBFS noise floor within 0.73 dB (the 16-bit design 33.3 dB high), for 10 cells more than a 16-bit design; rivals 709 / 645 / 408 cells.
findings.status_detail: one program, not repeated by anyone (wave 15, no critic); RTL bit-exact on 106,496 samples; netlist simulation unfinished

findings.statement: A 4,096-point streaming FFT fits the iCE40-UP5K: 4,849 cells (92 %), 30.9 MHz over 12 seeds, 47.7 dB SQNR; a capability whose only rivals are ablations.
findings.status_detail: one critic

findings.statement: A 4,096-point streaming WHT with its adders and multiplexers in the UP5K's 8 idle DSP blocks takes 253 against 633 cells (-60 %), about 58 MHz; for slow uses a folded design is smaller still (189 cells).
findings.status_detail: one critic
supersedes: 246 against 633 cells at 60.5 MHz; 8k/16k points as a capability

findings.statement: Feeding the bit that a halving butterfly drops into the sum's carry-in gains about 6 dB of signal-to-noise for 6-13 cells (free on the UP5K's DSP carry-in pin); the baseline gets it too.
findings.status_detail: one critic

findings.statement: The one-guard radix-4 NTT schedule in an FPGA NTT datapath: -18.5 % LUT4 / -14.7 % slices for the fabric of one radix-4 group on ECP5-25F (DSP products excluded).
findings.status_detail: one program, not repeated by anyone (a probe)

findings.statement: A fast-FIR structure across frames in a telescope filter bank needs 21 instead of 28 multiplies per two outputs at 14 taps per branch (-25 %), exact.
findings.status_detail: one program, not repeated by anyone (a probe)

findings.statement: xk265's HEVC interpolators as DSP48E1 chains save 18.6 % LUTs and 18.2 % DSPs in the module against a fair rival but only 7.6 % of the motion estimation's LUTs (below the bar; DSPs -17.8 %), synthesis only. The FME-level figures were measured with a SATD engine later found not to be a drop-in (hevc-fme-xrm-not-dropin), so they describe an incorrect design; the module-level figures do not depend on it.
findings.status_detail: one critic built the fair rival; synthesis only

findings.statement: The faster SATD engine used in the HEVC motion-estimation figures of waves 13-14 is not a drop-in replacement inside xk265: with it the FME writes different motion vectors for 88 % of entries, so the 73 % ECP5 placement and the Xilinx whole-FME figures were for an incorrect design; the correct design needs about 83 % of the ECP5-85F and 1080p30 needs 67.8 MHz against a 30.6 MHz pre-route estimate.
findings.status_detail: one program, not repeated by anyone (wave 15, no critic); it refutes the correctness of the earlier FME figures

findings.statement: int16 arithmetic for a Hadamard rotate-and-quantise on M4 NEON (claimed -22.3 / -26.6 % against fp32) is no gain: an fp16 kernel with the same plan is as fast or faster at equal quality; the gain was 16-bit lanes.
findings.status_detail: refuted by two critics (fp16 rival)
findings.refuted_by: an fp16 kernel with the same plan

open.question: Why does the SEAL port gain so much less on a non-Apple Arm core?
open.first_experiment: Time the new kernel and SEAL's lazy forward NTT level by level on a Neoverse N2 (GitHub Arm runners) and try -mcpu=neoverse-n2; if the lazy transform cannot gain, use the new code there only for the fully reduced transforms.

open.question: Does the fp64-FMA NTT give the same gain inside OpenFHE?
open.first_experiment: Route OpenFHE's NTT for primes below 2^50 through the floating-point method, run OpenFHE's unit tests, time its own CKKS benchmarks on the M4 and an Arm server runner.

open.question: A NEON build of FFTW for conda-forge and Homebrew users.
open.first_experiment: Rebuild conda-forge's recipe with --enable-neon in both precisions and the aarch64 host triple, run FFTW's tests/check.pl, time the probe grid and pyFFTW with the library swapped in.

open.question: Does the packed filter bank close timing in AMD's tools?
open.first_experiment: Place and route one lane and one slice in Vivado at 200-250 MHz; compare with AMD's FIR Compiler.

open.question: Do Lattice's own tools already fold multiplexers into carry cells?
open.first_experiment: Synthesise the folded and gated generic FFTs with Lattice Radiant on CrossLink-NX; if Radiant folds them, the gain is gone.

open.question: Does the convolve kernel survive a critic, and can it be made multi-process safe?
open.first_experiment: Have a critic rebuild the baselines; add a C FFT overlap-save above about 450 taps and the per-cluster try-lock; time 1, 4 and 8 Python processes.

open.question: What does the M4's second (efficiency-cluster) matrix unit add?
open.first_experiment: Time the batched complex128 FFT on the E-cluster unit alone, then one P-cluster plus one E-cluster thread plus NEON threads against all-NEON on all ten cores.

open.question: The optics step as a real split-step loop.
open.first_experiment: Natural-order output inside the kernels and a 100-step split-step loop, timed against scipy.fft with all workers and FFTW's threaded 2-D plan.

open.question: Is pocketfft's batched vector path fixable for large rows?
open.first_experiment: Cap the batched buffer at the L1 size and time 64 x 4,096 complex128 again.

open.question: What do the small-FPGA designs cost in power?
open.first_experiment: A switching-activity estimate with the open flow for the folded UP5K FFT and its rivals, then one board measurement.

open.question: Can HEVC fractional motion estimation route on an ECP5-85F at a usable clock with the encoder's own SATD?
open.first_experiment: Pipeline the candidate-index path and the vertical filters (a cycle-exact latency-neutral split exists), then route with 5 seeds.

open.question: How much area does packing two real radar channels per FFT save?
open.first_experiment: Place and route the packed and unpacked chains with 5 seeds each and write the area table.
